author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.
Explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to systemic versus pulmonary pressure demands.
Describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: Exterior Orientation of the Heart
modules.description: An intact and a cutaway human heart appear side by side. Students rotate both models together and learn the gross anatomical orientation, including why left and right are described from the patient's perspective.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Orient the heart anatomically with apex pointing down and to the left.
Distinguish the intact exterior view from the cutaway interior view.
Explain why the anatomical left and right are reversed relative to the viewer's perspective.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the two heart models and welcomes the student, establishing the exterior/interior pairing that anchors the whole lab.
clips.narration: Welcome to our exploration of the human heart. In front of you are two models of the same organ: on the left, an intact heart showing its exterior surface and great vessels; on the right, a cutaway with the anterior wall removed so we can see inside.

clips.changeMeaning: Both hearts slowly rotate together so students can appreciate the three-dimensional apex-down orientation from all angles.
clips.narration: The heart sits in the chest with its pointed apex directed downward and toward the left. Grab either model to rotate them and view the heart from any angle.

components.text: Patient's RIGHT is on your LEFT

clips.changeMeaning: Adds an orientation reminder label clarifying that left and right are named from the patient's perspective, a common source of confusion.
clips.narration: One key convention: the right and left sides of the heart are named from the patient's own orientation, not yours. So the chamber on YOUR left as you look at it is actually the patient's right side.

modules.description: Using the cutaway view, narration highlights each chamber, valve, and vessel in sequence, with labels appearing beside each structure and the intact heart highlighting the corresponding exterior landmark.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Name the four chambers in order: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle.
Name the four valves and the chambers or vessels they separate.
Name the major vessels: superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta.
Recognize the dual naming of the mitral/bicuspid valve.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the right atrium as the first chamber in the tour and names it, beginning the ordered structural inventory.
clips.narration: We begin our tour with the four chambers. Here is the right atrium, the upper-right receiving chamber that collects deoxygenated blood returning from the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the highlight to the right ventricle and updates the label, continuing the chamber sequence.
clips.narration: Below it, the right ventricle. This chamber pumps deoxygenated blood toward the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the left atrium and updates the label, moving to the oxygenated side of the heart.
clips.narration: On the opposite side, the left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood returning from the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the left ventricle, completing the four-chamber inventory and foreshadowing its role as the powerful systemic pump.
clips.narration: And the left ventricle, the powerhouse that drives blood out to the entire body. Notice already how much thicker its wall appears.

clips.changeMeaning: Transitions the tour to the valves, highlighting the tricuspid valve between the right atrium and right ventricle.
clips.narration: Now the four valves. Between the right atrium and right ventricle sits the tricuspid valve, with three leaflets.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the pulmonary (pulmonic) valve at the outflow of the right ventricle, continuing the valve sequence.
clips.narration: At the exit of the right ventricle is the pulmonary, or pulmonic, valve, guarding the pathway to the pulmonary trunk.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the mitral/bicuspid valve and explicitly notes its dual naming, addressing a clinically important vocabulary point.
clips.narration: Between the left atrium and left ventricle is the mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve because it has two leaflets. You will meet both names in clinical and anatomical settings.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the aortic valve at the left ventricular outflow, completing the four-valve set.
clips.narration: Finally, the aortic valve sits at the exit of the left ventricle, opening into the aorta.

components.text: Great Vessels: SVC, IVC, Pulmonary Arteries, Pulmonary Veins, Aorta

clips.changeMeaning: Transitions to the great vessels, highlighting the superior and inferior vena cava that deliver deoxygenated blood, then the pulmonary vessels and aorta.
clips.narration: Last, the great vessels. The superior and inferior vena cava return deoxygenated blood to the right atrium; the pulmonary arteries carry it to the lungs; the pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood back; and the aorta distributes it to the body.

modules.description: The cutaway heart fills with continuously flowing color-coded blood: blue for deoxygenated, red for oxygenated. The pulmonary and systemic circuits are labeled and highlighted in turn.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Associate blue with deoxygenated and red with oxygenated blood in the correct chambers and vessels.
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit as two distinct loops.
Explain why the right side pumps to the lungs and the left side pumps to the body.

components.scriptDescription: Animates a flowing particle stream along a predefined spline path to visualize blood movement. Inputs (set in inspector): a float flowSpeed controlling particle velocity, a Color streamColor for the blood, and a bool looping to repeat continuously. Output/effect: emits colored particles that travel along the assigned path each frame, giving a steady-state flow appearance. When disabled the stream stops emitting.

Animates a flowing particle stream along a predefined spline path to visualize blood movement. Inputs (set in inspector): a float flowSpeed controlling particle velocity, a Color streamColor for the blood, and a bool looping to repeat continuously. Output/effect: emits colored particles traveling along the assigned path each frame. When disabled the stream stops emitting.

clips.changeMeaning: Activates the blue deoxygenated stream on the right side of the heart, establishing the color convention for deoxygenated blood.
clips.narration: Watch the color-coded blood begin to flow. Blue marks deoxygenated blood, which fills the right side of the heart and the pulmonary arteries heading to the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Activates the red oxygenated stream on the left side, completing the two-color steady-state picture of circulation.
clips.narration: Red marks oxygenated blood, filling the left side of the heart, the pulmonary veins, and the aorta as it heads out to the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the pulmonary circuit as a distinct loop by dimming systemic flow, letting students isolate the right-heart-to-lung pathway.
clips.narration: Let's isolate the pulmonary circuit: the right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen. This is a short, low-pressure loop.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the systemic circuit by swapping which stream is active, contrasting the long high-pressure body loop with the pulmonary loop.
clips.narration: Now the systemic circuit: the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the entire body, a long, high-pressure loop, before it returns deoxygenated to the right side.

clips.changeMeaning: Re-enables both streams to show the dual circulation running together, cementing the two-loop-in-series relationship.
clips.narration: Together, these two loops form the dual circulation. The right heart drives the pulmonary circuit; the left heart drives the systemic circuit; and blood passes through both in series with every trip around the body.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Step-by-Step Red Blood Cell Trace
modules.description: A single red blood cell travels the full circulatory path one step at a time. Students advance the cell with the Next control; at each step it changes location, a label names the structure, and narration describes the event. The cell changes blue to red at the lungs.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace a blood cell through the complete pulmonary and systemic circuit in order.
Identify where in the path oxygenation occurs (lung capillaries).
Connect each chamber and valve transition to a cardiac event (contraction pushing blood forward).

clips.changeMeaning: Places the blue blood cell in the superior vena cava as the starting point of the trace, establishing it as deoxygenated.
clips.narration: Follow a single blood cell. It begins deoxygenated, colored blue, in the superior vena cava, returning from the upper body.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the cell into the right atrium, the first chamber, advancing the trace along its path.
clips.narration: The cell empties into the right atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: Advances the cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, tying the movement to atrial contraction.
clips.narration: The right atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Advances the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk on its way to the lungs, tying it to ventricular contraction.
clips.narration: The right ventricle contracts, pushing the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.

clips.changeMeaning: Sends the cell out the pulmonary arteries toward the lung capillaries, still blue, approaching the site of gas exchange.
clips.narration: The pulmonary arteries carry the still-deoxygenated cell toward the lung capillaries. Remember: pulmonary arteries are the exception that carry deoxygenated blood.

clips.changeMeaning: At the lung capillaries the cell visibly changes from blue to red as it loads oxygen, the pedagogical centerpiece of the trace.
clips.narration: In the lung capillaries the cell picks up oxygen and drops carbon dioxide. Watch it turn from blue to red.

clips.changeMeaning: Returns the now-red cell via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, reinforcing that pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.
clips.narration: Oxygen-rich blood returns through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium. Again the exception: pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.

clips.changeMeaning: Advances the cell through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, tying movement to left atrial contraction.
clips.narration: The left atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Ejects the cell through the aortic valve into the aorta as the left ventricle contracts, the final cardiac step before systemic distribution.
clips.narration: The powerful left ventricle contracts, driving the cell through the aortic valve into the aorta.

clips.changeMeaning: Sends the cell into systemic circulation and then returns it blue via the vena cava, closing the loop and inviting replay.
clips.narration: The aorta delivers the cell to the body's tissues, where it gives up oxygen and turns blue again, then returns through the systemic veins to the superior vena cava, completing the loop. Replay the trace as often as you like.

modules.description: Two horizontal cross-sections of the ventricles are shown side by side with scale markers. The thin right-ventricular wall and the thick left-ventricular wall are highlighted and labeled, and narration explains the functional reason.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare the right and left ventricular myocardial thickness and estimate the roughly three-to-one ratio.
Explain why the left ventricle wall is thicker in terms of systemic versus pulmonary pressure.
Relate wall thickness to the resistance each ventricle must overcome.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the two matched cross-sections cut at the same level, framing the direct comparison of ventricular walls.
clips.narration: Here are two cross-sections of the heart cut at the same horizontal level through the ventricles, so we can compare the walls directly.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the thin right-ventricular myocardium and labels its approximately three to five millimeter thickness.
clips.narration: On the left cross-section, the right ventricle. Its myocardium is thin, roughly three to five millimeters in a healthy adult.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the thick left-ventricular myocardium and labels its approximately ten to fifteen millimeter thickness, exposing the asymmetry.
clips.narration: On the right cross-section, the left ventricle. Its myocardium is far thicker, roughly ten to fifteen millimeters, about three times the right.

clips.changeMeaning: Slowly rotates both cross-sections together so students can confirm the thickness ratio from different angles.
clips.narration: Rotate the cross-sections to confirm the roughly three-to-one thickness ratio for yourself.

clips.changeMeaning: Delivers the functional explanation linking the left ventricle's thickness to the high-pressure systemic circuit.
clips.narration: The reason is functional. The right ventricle pumps blood only to the nearby lungs, a low-pressure circuit. The left ventricle must push blood through the entire body against much higher resistance, so it needs a far more muscular wall.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Valve Function and Backflow Prevention
modules.description: The cutaway heart returns with valves highlighted. Narration distinguishes atrioventricular from semilunar valves, and open/closed valve models swap to show how leaflets seal or clear the opening at each phase of the cardiac cycle.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Classify the four valves as atrioventricular (tricuspid, mitral) or semilunar (pulmonary, aortic).
Explain how each valve prevents backflow during a specific phase of the cardiac cycle.
State which valves are open and which are closed during ventricular contraction versus relaxation.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the two valve categories, framing the distinction between atrioventricular and semilunar valves.
clips.narration: The heart has two categories of valves. The atrioventricular valves, the tricuspid and mitral, sit between the atria and ventricles. The semilunar valves, the pulmonary and aortic, sit between the ventricles and their outflow arteries.

clips.changeMeaning: Shows the open atrioventricular valve model to illustrate how leaflets clear the path during ventricular filling.
clips.narration: During ventricular relaxation, the atrioventricular valves are open, letting blood flow from the atria into the ventricles. Notice how the leaflets swing clear of the opening.

clips.changeMeaning: Swaps to the closed atrioventricular valve model to show leaflets sealing shut during ventricular contraction, preventing backflow.
clips.narration: When the ventricles contract, the atrioventricular valves snap shut, their leaflets sealing the opening so blood cannot flow backward into the atria.

clips.changeMeaning: Reuses the open valve model to represent semilunar valves opening during ventricular contraction, contrasting their timing with the AV valves.
clips.narration: At that same moment, the semilunar valves open. As the ventricles contract, blood is forced out through the pulmonary and aortic valves.

clips.changeMeaning: Swaps to the closed valve model for the semilunar valves during ventricular relaxation, showing they prevent backflow from the arteries.
clips.narration: When the ventricles relax, the semilunar valves close, preventing blood in the aorta and pulmonary trunk from falling back into the ventricles.

components.text: Valves Alternate to Force One-Way Flow

clips.changeMeaning: Summarizes the reciprocal timing of the two valve sets across the cardiac cycle to consolidate the concept.
clips.narration: The key pattern: during ventricular contraction the atrioventricular valves are closed and the semilunar valves are open; during relaxation the reverse is true. This alternation keeps blood always moving in one direction.

modules.description: The unlabeled cutaway heart appears. The system highlights a chamber, valve, or vessel and presents candidate names; students select the correct one, receiving confirmation or correction after each choice.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recall and identify chambers, valves, and vessels without labels present.
Reinforce mapping between highlighted structure and correct anatomical name.
Self-assess mastery of the structural inventory.

clips.changeMeaning: Presents the first quiz item by highlighting the right atrium and offering three candidate names.
clips.narration: Let's test your recall. The labels are gone. Which structure is highlighted now? Select your answer.

clips.changeMeaning: Confirms the right-atrium answer and moves the highlight to a valve for the next question.
clips.narration: Correct, that is the right atrium. Now for a valve. Which valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle?

clips.changeMeaning: Confirms the mitral valve answer and highlights a great vessel for the final sampled question.
clips.narration: Correct, the mitral or bicuspid valve. Last, identify this large vessel leaving the left ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Confirms the aorta answer and invites the student to replay the quiz cycling through all structures.
clips.narration: Correct, the aorta. The full quiz cycles through all four chambers, all four valves, and every major vessel. Replay it to strengthen your identification skills.

modules.description: Given a starting position in the circuit, students select the next structure in the path. The quiz steps through the full pulmonary and systemic circuit, emphasizing the pulmonary artery/vein oxygenation reversal.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Order the structures of the circulatory path correctly from any starting point.
Distinguish pulmonary arteries (deoxygenated) from pulmonary veins (oxygenated).
Recover from errors using directional reasoning about circulation.

components.text: What comes next in the path?
Blood is in the RIGHT ATRIUM. Next structure?

clips.changeMeaning: Poses the first flow question from the right atrium, presenting next-structure options for the student to choose.
clips.narration: A unit of blood has just entered the right atrium. Which structure does it flow to next? Select your answer.

components.text: Blood is in the RIGHT VENTRICLE. Next structure?

clips.changeMeaning: Confirms right ventricle as the correct next step and advances the cell, then asks the crucial pulmonary artery question.
clips.narration: Correct, through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. Now the tricky one: from the right ventricle, blood is pumped toward the lungs. Which vessel carries it, and does that vessel carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?

components.text: Blood is heading to the LUNGS. Where does it return?

clips.changeMeaning: Reinforces the pulmonary artery/vein reversal and advances the cell toward the lungs, addressing the most common misconception.
clips.narration: Correct, the pulmonary arteries, and unlike every other artery, they carry deoxygenated blood. This reversal is the classic trap: pulmonary arteries carry blood away from the heart to the lungs to be oxygenated.

clips.changeMeaning: Confirms the return to the left atrium via pulmonary veins, turns the cell red, and completes the sampled circuit with a replay invitation.
clips.narration: Correct. After oxygenation in the lungs, blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, now red. From there it passes the mitral valve, the left ventricle, the aortic valve, and out the aorta to the body. Replay the quiz to walk the entire circuit yourself.

modules.description: A summary screen lists the five concept areas of the lab. Each area is highlighted in turn as the narration reviews it, consolidating the full arc of the experience.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recall the five concept areas covered in the lab.
Integrate structure, circulation, wall thickness, and valve function into a coherent whole.
Self-identify areas that may need review.

components.text: 1. Chambers, valves, vessels  2. Pulmonary + systemic circuits  3. Path of a unit of blood  4. Ventricular wall thickness  5. Valve function & backflow
>> 1. Chambers, valves, vessels  2. Pulmonary + systemic circuits  3. Path of a unit of blood  4. Ventricular wall thickness  5. Valve function & backflow

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the first concept area, the structural inventory, beginning the ordered review of all five topics.
clips.narration: Let's review. First, the structural inventory: four chambers, four valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.

components.text: 1. Chambers, valves, vessels  >> 2. Pulmonary + systemic circuits  3. Path of a unit of blood  4. Ventricular wall thickness  5. Valve function & backflow

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts the highlight to the dual-circuit concept, reviewing the pulmonary versus systemic distinction.
clips.narration: Second, the dual-circuit organization: the pulmonary circuit carries blood from the right heart to the lungs, and the systemic circuit carries blood from the left heart to the body.

components.text: 1. Chambers, valves, vessels  2. Pulmonary + systemic circuits  >> 3. Path of a unit of blood  4. Ventricular wall thickness  5. Valve function & backflow

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the blood-path concept, reviewing the ordered trace through the full circulation.
clips.narration: Third, the path of a unit of blood: right atrium, tricuspid, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral, left ventricle, aortic valve, and out to the body.

components.text: 1. Chambers, valves, vessels  2. Pulmonary + systemic circuits  3. Path of a unit of blood  >> 4. Ventricular wall thickness  5. Valve function & backflow

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the wall-thickness concept, reviewing the functional reason for ventricular asymmetry.
clips.narration: Fourth, wall thickness: the left ventricle is roughly three times thicker than the right because it must overcome the high pressure of the systemic circuit.

components.text: 1. Chambers, valves, vessels  2. Pulmonary + systemic circuits  3. Path of a unit of blood  4. Ventricular wall thickness  >> 5. Valve function & backflow

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the final valve-function concept and closes the lab with an encouraging summary.
clips.narration: And fifth, valve function: the atrioventricular and semilunar valves alternate opening and closing to prevent backflow and keep blood moving one way. You now have a complete picture of the heart's structure and the journey of blood through it. Well done.
